what_happened: The operator closed pull request #131 by hand and left a comment saying #132 superseded it. The content of job jbt9 had already reached main inside #132, because the exemption job was cut on top of jbt9's unmerged branch. Athena does not close a pull request whose work landed through a later one, so #131 would have stayed open and redundant.
cause: Athena allows a job to be built on an earlier unmerged job's branch but does not record that dependency or link the pull requests. Its lifecycle treats each pull request as independent. When the later pull request merges, nothing detects that it carries the earlier commits, so the earlier job and PR stay open until a person notices. The gap was already known (6ejp) and is still unfixed. It has now recurred in consecutive jobs, and each time the operator cleans up by hand.
prevention: Record the base job or branch when a job is cut on top of unmerged work. After any pull request merges, run a check that finds open pull requests whose head commits are all reachable from main. Close each one automatically with a comment naming the merging PR, and mark its job as superseded or done. This one rule covers the whole class, whichever jobs are stacked.
proposed_request: When a pull request merges, Athena should find any other open Athena pull requests whose commits are now all contained in main, close each with a comment naming the merging pull request, and mark the corresponding jobs as superseded. Record the base job whenever a job is built on an unmerged earlier job so the link is explicit. Acceptance: with job B stacked on unmerged job A, merging B's pull request closes A's pull request automatically with a comment and sets A's job state to superseded, with no operator action. A test covers this stacked case, and a pull request with commits not in main stays open.
